questions.question: Why does putStrLn Hello fail with 'Variable not in scope: Hello' rather than simply printing the word Hello?
options: putStrLn only accepts numbers, not words
Hello has no quotation marks, so Haskell treats it as an identifier to look up rather than as literal text — and no such identifier has been defined
Hello is spelled with a capital letter, which putStrLn cannot accept
This is a GHC bug that only affects the word Hello specifically
questions.explanation: Quotation marks are the only thing that makes a word a String literal. With no quotes, Hello can only mean one thing to the parser: 'look up a name called Hello.' Since nothing by that name exists, GHC reports exactly that — a missing variable — before putStrLn is ever reached.
optionFeedback: putStrLn's whole job is displaying String values, whether they contain letters, digits, or punctuation; the type of characters inside the string is not the issue here.
Correct. This is the rule stated above with no exceptions: an unquoted word is always a name to look up, and Hello was never defined as one.

Capitalisation changes what kind of identifier Haskell expects (a data constructor rather than an ordinary name) — it does not cause this particular error, and lowercase hello would fail exactly the same way, just with a different explanation once looked up.
This is standard, fully documented behaviour that happens for any undefined identifier — try putStrLn anythingUndefined and the same class of error appears.

questions.question: Why does length "Hello" work (giving 5) while length 'H' would be rejected by the type checker?
options: length only works on words longer than one letter
String is a list of characters, and length counts the elements of a list; a bare Char is a single value, not a list, so there is nothing for length to count
'H' is not a valid Char literal
length secretly converts 'H' into "H" first, so both should work identically
questions.explanation: length's job is counting elements in a list. "Hello" :: String, and String is defined as [Char] — a list — so length "Hello" counts its five Char elements. 'H' :: Char is one value, not a list at all, so length has nothing to apply to.
optionFeedback: length "H" (a one-character String) works fine and reports 1 — length is not restricted by word length, only by whether it is given a list.
Correct. This is exactly the structural difference the lesson is building toward: String is [Char], a list; Char is one element, not a list.
'H' is a perfectly valid Char literal — single quotes around exactly one character is the definition of a valid Char.
There is no automatic conversion from Char to String anywhere in this rule; the two remain distinct types unless you explicitly build a one-element list, ['H'], which does equal "H".

questions.question: f x y = (f x) y is given as the rule for how application groups. Applied to square 3 4 (imagining square took two arguments), what would this mean?
options: Apply square to the pair (3, 4) at once
First apply square to 3, then apply whatever that produces to 4
Apply square to 4 first, then to 3
It is meaningless; functions can only take one argument written this way
questions.explanation: Left-associativity means square 3 4 is (square 3) 4: square is applied to 3 first, and the result of that is then applied to 4 — never the reverse, and never as a single combined pair.
optionFeedback: That is how a tuple argument would be written explicitly, as square (3, 4) — space-separated application never bundles arguments into a pair automatically.
Correct. This is exactly the left-grouping rule: (square 3) 4, applied strictly in the order written.
Application always proceeds left to right in the order the arguments are written, never reversed.
This is precisely how Haskell writes a function taking two arguments, one space at a time — square 3 4 is completely ordinary syntax, not an error.

questions.question: A student writes 'hello' (single quotes) expecting it to work like a short string. What specifically goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong; single and double quotes are interchangeable in Haskell
Char is defined to hold exactly one character; 'hello' has five characters, which cannot fit inside a Char literal
hello is not a valid identifier name
Single quotes are reserved for comments in Haskell
questions.explanation: Single quotes specifically construct a Char, and Char's whole definition is 'exactly one character.' Five characters between single quotes is simply too many for what that literal form is allowed to hold — it is rejected as a parse error, not a type error, because it is invalid before types even come into it.
optionFeedback: They are not interchangeable: double quotes build a String (any length, including zero), single quotes build a Char (exactly one character) — different literal forms for different types.
Correct. This is the structural reason from Section 2: Char cannot represent more than one character, full stop.
hello would be a perfectly ordinary — if undefined — identifier; that is not the problem with 'hello' specifically, which fails regardless of whether hello happens to be defined elsewhere.
Comments use -- or {- -}, covered in the previous lesson; quotes of either kind have nothing to do with comments.
